pages.name: Switch on
pages.text: A 24 V supply, a 0.5 H coil and 10 Ω sit in one loop. The switch closes. Round the loop the voltages add up, so `24 = L di/dt + R i`. At first the current is 0, so the coil takes all 24 V. The current climbs at 24 ÷ 0.5 = 48 A a second. As it grows, the resistor takes `10 i` volts. That leaves the coil less, so the climb slows. The curve bends over.

A loop: supply E, a two-way switch closed onto the supply, coil L and resistor R. at 0 A: (24 minus 10 times 0) divided by 0.5 equals 48 A a second. A bar shares the 24 volts: the resistor takes 98 per cent, the coil the rest. A rider climbs the curve from 0 amps. Its rate arrow starts steep and flattens.

pages.name: Where the climb stops
pages.task: The climb stops where the rate is zero. What current is that?
pages.why: The rate is zero when the coil's share of the 24 V is zero. Then the resistor takes all of it. So `10 i = 24`, and the current is 24 ÷ 10 = 2.4 A. That is the [[steady current]], `E ÷ R`. `L` is not in it.

pages.alt: Rule: L d i by d t equals E minus R i. E equals 24 V, L equals 0.5 H, R equals 10 ohms. A loop: supply E, a two-way switch closed onto the supply, coil L and resistor R. rate zero: 24 equals 10 i, so i equals 24 divided by 10 equals 2.4 A. rate zero at 2.4 A.

pages.name: The steady line and the gap
pages.text: A dashed line marks the [[steady state]], `E ÷ R` = 2.4 A. There the current stops changing. The shaded strip is the [[gap]], the current minus 2.4 A. Below the line it is negative. Take 10 out of the top of the rule, and it reads `di/dt = (2.4 − i) ÷ 0.05`. The 0.05 s is 0.5 ÷ 10, which is `L ÷ R`. So the rate is the gap's size ÷ 0.05 s. At 1.2 A the gap has halved, and so has the rate.
pages.alt: Rule: L d i by d t equals E minus R i. E equals 24 V, L equals 0.5 H, R equals 10 ohms. A loop: supply E, a two-way switch closed onto the supply, coil L and resistor R. d i by d t equals (24 minus 10 i) divided by 0.5 equals (2.4 minus i) divided by 0.05. 0.05 s equals 0.5 divided by 10, which is L divided by R. at 0 A: (2.4 minus 0) divided by 0.05 equals 48 A a second. Rate arrows at 0 amps and at 1.2 amps. Where the gap has halved, the arrow is half as steep in amps a second. steady E divided by R equals 2.4 A. gap minus 2.4 A, the full rate. gap minus 1.2 A, half the rate.

pages.name: The rate at 1.2 A
pages.task: The current has reached 1.2 A. How fast is it climbing there?
pages.why: The rate is the gap's size ÷ 0.05 s. At 1.2 A the gap's size is 1.2 A. So the rate is 1.2 ÷ 0.05 = 24 A a second. That is half the starting 48, because the gap has halved.
pages.alt: Rule: L d i by d t equals E minus R i. E equals 24 V, L equals 0.5 H, R equals 10 ohms. A loop: supply E, a two-way switch closed onto the supply, coil L and resistor R. (2.4 minus 1.2) divided by 0.05 equals 24 A a second. steady 2.4 A. at 1.2 A, the gap is minus 1.2 A.

pages.name: The gap at each τ
pages.text: The marks along the bottom sit one `τ = L ÷ R` = 0.05 s apart. The steady line holds still, so the gap changes just as fast as the current. So the gap follows the discharge's rule: its rate is −gap ÷ `τ`. So each `τ` keeps the same share of it, 0.368. At the marks it reads −2.4, −0.883, −0.325 and −0.119 A. It never quite closes. A straight line at the starting rate meets the dashed line at one `τ`. Anywhere, the gap is 0.368 of its size one `τ` before.
pages.alt: Rule: L d i by d t equals E minus R i. E equals 24 V, L equals 0.5 H, R equals 10 ohms. A loop: supply E, a two-way switch closed onto the supply, coil L and resistor R. Amber bars show the gap at each tau mark, each 0.368 of the one before. The marker sits at 0.15 seconds. steady 2.4 A. gap.

pages.name: After one τ
pages.task: What is the current after one `τ`, at 0.05 s?
pages.why: One `τ` keeps 0.368 of the gap. So the gap goes from −2.4 A to −2.4 × 0.368 = −0.883 A. The current is 2.4 − 0.883 = 1.52 A. It has closed 0.632 of the gap.

pages.name: Split
pages.text: Here the curve comes apart. One piece is the flat steady line at 2.4 A. The other is the dying gap, `−2.4 e^(−t/0.05)`, drawn below the axis. Add the two, height by height, and you get the current back. The supply and `R` set the steady line. The start sets the gap, the [[transient]], and it dies away. With a sine supply the steady part is a sine. For a resistor and capacitor it is what the impedance method gives.
pages.alt: Rule: L d i by d t equals E minus R i. E equals 24 V, L equals 0.5 H, R equals 10 ohms. The current splits into the steady line at 2.4 amps and the gap, drawn below the axis. Amber bars of equal length hang from the steady line and from zero. steady line 2.4 A. i equals 2.4 minus 2.4 e to the power minus t/0.05. gap minus 2.4 e to the power minus t/0.05.

pages.name: Another route
pages.text: A second route is the [[integrating factor]]. Write the rule with `di/dt` on its own: `di/dt + i ÷ 0.05 = 48`. Multiply both sides by `e^(t/0.05)`, whose slope is itself ÷ 0.05. A product's slope is each part's slope times the other part, added. So the left side is now the slope of `i e^(t/0.05)`. Integrate both sides: `e^(t/0.05)` integrates to 0.05 `e^(t/0.05)`, and 48 × 0.05 = 2.4. Divide by `e^(t/0.05)` to get `i = 2.4 + c e^(−t/0.05)`. Starting from 0 A makes `c` = −2.4. It is the same curve.

pages.name: The supply drops
pages.task: The current sits steady at 2.4 A. Then the supply drops to 12 V, so the new steady line is 1.2 A. Which formula does the current now follow?
pages.why: The new steady value is 12 ÷ 10 = 1.2 A. The current starts at 2.4 A, so the gap starts at 2.4 − 1.2 = +1.2 A. It dies with the same `τ`, 0.05 s. So `i = 1.2 + 1.2 e^(−t/0.05)`. It starts at 2.4 A and settles on 1.2 A.

pages.name: Your own run
pages.text: `E` and `R` move the steady line. `R` also sets `τ`. The start moves only the gap, above or below the line. When the switch flips mid-run, the supply drops out. The loop closes through `R`, so the line drops to 0. Whatever the settings, the gap keeps 0.368 of itself from one `τ` mark to the next. The one exception is across the flip, where the line jumps.
pages.alt: Rule: L d i by d t equals E minus R i. L equals 0.5 H. A loop: supply E, a two-way switch closed onto the supply, coil L and resistor R. E is 24 volts, R is 10 ohms and the start is 0 amps. The supply stays on. steady line.

pages.name: A bigger coil
pages.task: Swap the 0.5 H coil for a 1 H coil. The supply and resistor stay the same. What happens to the current?

pages.name: One curve for all three
pages.text: The same shape fits a motor running up to speed. It fits a tank filling too, if its outflow keeps in step with its level. A ship answering its rudder is often modelled this way. Each has a steady value and a `τ`. Draw time in `τ`, and the value as its share of the way there. Then they all draw one curve: 63.2% at one `τ`, 86.5% at two, 95.0% at three and 99.3% at five. Coil, motor or tank, it is the same curve.

pages.name: A motor runs up
pages.task: A motor's speed `n` follows `dn/dt = (1500 − n) ÷ 0.2`, in rpm and seconds. It starts from rest. What is its speed after 0.4 s?
pages.why: The steady speed is 1500 rpm and `τ` is 0.2 s. So 0.4 s is two `τ`. The gap starts at −1500 rpm. Two `τ` keep 0.368 × 0.368 of it, which is −203 rpm. So the speed is 1500 − 203 = 1297 rpm.
pages.alt: Rule: d n by d t equals (1500 minus n) divided by 0.2. two tau : minus 1500 times 0.368 times 0.368 equals minus 203 rpm. n equals 1500 minus 203 equals 1297 rpm. 1297 rpm. steady 1500 rpm. after 0.4 s.

pages.name: A tank settles
pages.task: A tank's level `h` follows `dh/dt = (2 − h) ÷ 50`, in metres and seconds. The level starts at 3 m. What is it after 50 s?
pages.why: The steady level is 2 m and `τ` is 50 s. The gap starts at 3 − 2 = +1 m. After one `τ` it keeps 0.368 of that. So the level is 2 + 0.368 = 2.37 m. It falls towards 2 m, not to zero.
pages.alt: Rule: d h by d t equals (2 minus h) divided by 50. one tau : the gap keeps 1 times 0.368 equals 0.368 m. h equals 2 plus 0.368 equals 2.37 m. 2.37 m. steady 2 m. after 50 s. plus 1 m.
